judge_output.rationale: Carrigan (2009ApJ...698.2075C) already tested whether infrared excesses follow a single blackbody shape, using IRAS LRS spectra at 100-600 K and longer wavelengths. The card itself describes its method as a transfer of that test to SPHEREx. Hephaistos II (2024MNRAS.531..695S) fitted a photosphere plus a single-blackbody excess, but to broadband Gaia/2MASS/WISE photometry. Chen et al. (2006ApJS..166..351C) compared a single-temperature model with a continuous-disk model for natural debris disks at 5.5-35 um. None of the listed works fits a log-normal temperature width or Bayes factor to 2.5-5 um SPHEREx spectra, or makes a population-level claim about the fraction of narrow excesses.

closest_prior.relation: Fitted blackbodies to IRAS LRS spectra of about 250,000 sources to find single-temperature 100-600 K excesses; this is the same spectral-shape test at lower resolution, longer wavelengths and cooler temperatures, without a fitted temperature-width parameter.

Fitted photosphere-plus-blackbody models to Gaia/2MASS/WISE photometry of 5 million sources and kept seven M-dwarf candidates; it used broadband SEDs and did not test single versus distributed temperature.

Compared single-temperature blackbody fits with continuous-disk fits for 59 debris disks in Spitzer IRS 5.5-35 um spectra, finding many are better fit by a single temperature; this bears on the natural-confounder side of the card at longer wavelengths.
Set upper limits on partial Dyson spheres from Gaia DR2/AllWISE colour cuts; photometric colours only, with no spectral-shape or temperature-width analysis.

judge_output.what_would_make_it_open: No listed work measures sigma_lnT and single-versus-distributed-temperature Bayes factors on 2.5-5 um SPHEREx spectra of a parallax-selected stellar excess sample, calibrates them on known debris disks, YSOs and brown dwarfs, or tests whether at least 99 per cent of excesses are broad and whether the narrow ones lack molecular bands.
